ORIGINAL USMLE-STYLE PRACTICE

Imaging in uncomplicated outpatient pneumonia

A healthy 6-year-old has fever and focal crackles consistent with uncomplicated community-acquired pneumonia. He has normal oxygen saturation, no significant work of breathing and can take oral fluids. Which investigation strategy is most appropriate?

  1. Clinical management without a routine chest radiograph
  2. Obtain chest CT to define the affected segment
  3. Obtain a chest radiograph before prescribing any antibiotic
  4. Obtain serial radiographs to establish progression
  5. Perform bronchoscopy to identify the pathogen
Answer and explanation

Clinical management without a routine chest radiograph

A chest radiograph is not routinely required for a well child with a straightforward outpatient presentation.

Option explanations

Clinical management without a routine chest radiograph: A chest radiograph is not routinely required for a well child with a straightforward outpatient presentation.

Obtain chest CT to define the affected segment: CT is disproportionate for uncomplicated clinically diagnosed pneumonia and adds radiation.

Obtain a chest radiograph before prescribing any antibiotic: Routine imaging is unnecessary in a stable child with an uncomplicated clinical presentation.

Obtain serial radiographs to establish progression: Serial imaging is not needed when disease is uncomplicated and the child can be followed clinically.

Perform bronchoscopy to identify the pathogen: Bronchoscopy is invasive and is not the routine diagnostic approach for uncomplicated outpatient pneumonia.
